reason: Inserting a named result in the main design is part of creating and wiring endpoints. The UDF result port has a different scope.
Pattern matching and tokenization constrain built-in scalar/sequence function behavior; bracket syntax is not a separate callable.
The request/response component owns header, route and optional body structures.
Selecting fields from an HTTP response is the existing call workflow, independent of the example endpoint.
The distinctive step is declaring the feed response on a network call; RSS does not require a new connector here.
Supplying a constant argument to a SOAP operation is an instance of the existing live-service family.
The calendar call consumes a grant and token obtained through a credential; simple request/response wiring cannot assess authorization.
Installing a trusted issuer into a Linux trust store changes the host, not the mapping.
Importing a root into a Windows store belongs to Windows trust administration.
Choosing a user or computer certificate store in MMC is host administration.
Exporting a Windows certificate for another OS transfers deployment material outside the design.
Standalone run uses --certificatespath for the directory containing the client PEM. PEM preparation and access to the key are external prerequisites.
Availability of a certificate to the Windows execution account is a store prerequisite. Selection on the service component is covered separately at 781.
Submitting a design to the assistant and receiving suggested wires is a distinct editor operation. Blank-project wiring does not describe that exchange.
Reading actual child names as values requires name-bearing ports. Static XML field iteration and dynamic filenames do not expose those names.
Selecting allowed child content by type requires a schema-dependent projection. Merely exposing the child's name cannot provide typed fields.
The element-name-to-attribute workflow consumes the same name-bearing port as 808. Ordinary iteration determines row count, not the name value.
Imported versus local definitions and same-name precedence determine which credential a mapping uses. Connection setup alone has no such scope rule.
Configuring an authorization grant and using its token can be tested separately from name lookup and from ordinary HTTP body wiring.
The runtime supplies values for a credential name to the standalone invocation; deployment.host-api owns invocation parameters, not secret storage.

The designer controls inclusion of populated sensitive fields when deploying a mapping or a standalone credential. FlowForce storage, job overrides and access permissions are separate server operations.
The Credentials Manager command deploys one selected credential to a server path independently of its mapping. Job reuse and permission to use the object belong to the server.
Authentication inputs are runtime parameters on the service request. This case does not create an OAuth grant or resolve a stored credential by name.
The stored username/password option is a legacy authentication mode on the service call, distinct from a reusable named credential.
Selecting a stylesheet changes report content (e.g., call graph versus impact). The existing generate-documentation command ID identifies the menu action, not the generated report.
The custom documentation layout is authored in StyleVision against the documentation schema; that editor is outside the native mapping profile.
Choosing a resource configuration binds a logical name to a physical resource. A relocatable file path or release catalog is not a selectable configuration.
Each configuration can hold a different file or database binding for the same alias. This is setup for the resolver, not a new driver.
Switching the XML input by configuration keeps the design reference stable, unlike changing the component filename.
The alias can select an output directory. The independent temporary/permanent output setting still applies.
Switching a database through its configured alias is separable from connecting through that database's driver.
The designer can register a transformation result and bind a selected output per configuration. Launching the mapping and displaying its result in XMLSpy are external consumer actions.
The operation under assessment here is substitution into generated output, including the RaptorXML batch wrapper; resource definition is covered by 852.
The standalone server needs definitions to resolve preserved references in an execution file. This is host provisioning for the headless run.
A FlowForce resource is a permissioned server object. Server authorization is outside the mapping's resource-alias binding.
Selecting matching IDE and add-in bitness is a Visual Studio installation prerequisite.
Installing the mapping plug-in in a supported Eclipse platform is IDE setup. The canonical Java/Eclipse ActiveX prerequisite describes a different integration.
Selecting an Eclipse perspective changes the workbench where the design is edited.
Showing commands according to the active Eclipse editor is workbench routing, not a new mapping operation.
The Eclipse project type configures workspace integration; it is distinct from a mapping project file.
Creating the mapping design is the same authoring outcome from an Eclipse entry point. Other project-file choices do not add another kind of mapping.
Importing dependent files into an Eclipse project concerns workspace membership, distinct from resolving those files inside the mapping.
The builder and nature configure Eclipse project builds. Selecting a target code language in the design does not configure the workbench.
Installing plug-in development tools and extending an Eclipse plug-in are IDE development workflows.
The XSLT 1 serializer controls HTML character representation; the observed spelling belongs to the target processor's profile.
XSLT 2 backwards-compatibility behavior constrains that backend and does not define a second source mapping primitive.
XQuery engine namespace bindings and accepted encodings are backend-specific environment rules.
The Java namespace identifies the extension class referenced from an expression; this is external-function resolution.
A JAR location further qualifies the external implementation, rather than introducing a different expression result type.
The Java constructor convention is part of external invocation and can yield a wrapped receiver.
Class-qualified static calls do not consume an instance. The external-call family owns this dispatch distinction.
Instance dispatch consumes a receiver; this qualifies how the external method is called.
The selected Java signature determines conversion from the expression argument at the external boundary.
Conversion of a Java result back to XPath is the return direction of the external-call boundary.
The .NET constructor convention specifies object creation for an extension call.
Exact public static name matching constrains .NET extension resolution.
A .NET instance method uses the supplied object even when it takes no ordinary arguments.
Conversion to a .NET parameter depends on the selected signature; this is host argument marshalling.
Converting the .NET return type back to an expression value belongs to the external-call boundary.
Inline script placement describes where an XSLT extension implementation is declared; it does not imply arbitrary script execution support.
Memory sizing for an in-memory desktop editor is a platform requirement, not a mapped data operation.
Well-formedness and schema validation are XML parsing contracts. The page also describes the vendor engine, but it does not establish Ferrule validator coverage.
Rendering a glyph depends on installed fonts. It is distinct from a mapping's Unicode encoding and preservation behavior.
Requesting an evaluation key initiates application licensing traffic, outside mapping network operations.
